**Design Memo: Local-First Note-Taking App**

**1. Data Model for Notes, Tags, and Links**

The app will use a simple, relational data model. Each note is stored as a document with a unique ID, title, content, creation timestamp, and last modified timestamp. Notes can be linked to other notes via a bidirectional "link" relationship, stored as a JSON array of note IDs. Tags are stored as a separate collection of tag objects, each with a unique ID, name, and color. Notes can have multiple tags, represented as a JSON array of tag IDs. This model allows for flexible linking and tagging, while maintaining data integrity.

**Example:**  
Note A (ID: "note1") has tags ["tag1", "tag2"] and is linked to Note B (ID: "note2"). Tag "tag1" has ID "tag1" and color "blue".

**2. Full-Text Search Offline**

Full-text search should be performed locally using an indexed search engine, such as SQLite with FTS4 or a lightweight in-memory search index. When a note is created or modified, its content is indexed by keywords, and search queries are executed against this local index. The index should be updated incrementally to ensure real-time relevance. Search results are displayed in the app without requiring a network connection.

**Example:**  
A user searches for "project deadline" and the app returns all notes containing those keywords, based on the local index.

**3. Conflict-Resolution Strategy for Syncing**

When two devices edit the same note while offline, the app should use a last-write-wins (LWW) strategy with a timestamp-based resolution. Each note includes a version number and timestamp. When syncing, the app compares timestamps and replaces the note with the most recent version. If timestamps are equal, the note with the higher version number is kept. This ensures consistency without requiring user intervention for minor conflicts.

The app will use a simple, relational data model with three main entities: **Notes**, **Tags**, and **Links**.

- **Notes** have a unique ID, title, content, creation date, and last modified date.
- **Tags** are also uniquely identified and have a name and a color (optional).
- **Links** connect notes to each other or to tags, with a source note ID, target note ID, or target tag ID, and a type (e.g., "related", "contains", "tagged").

Example:  
Note A (ID: 123) is tagged with "Project" (Tag ID: 456), and Note B (ID: 789) is linked to Note A as "related".

---

Full-text search should be performed locally using an indexed search engine that supports offline operation. Each note’s content should be indexed in a local database (e.g., SQLite or a similar embedded database), with fields such as title, content, and tags included in the index.

The search should support fuzzy matching, partial matches, and tag-based filtering. Search results should be sorted by relevance and date modified.

Example:  
A user searches for "project deadline" and gets results including Note A (which contains "project deadline") and Note B (which is tagged with "project" and mentions "deadline").

---

When two devices are offline and both edit the same note, a **last-write-wins (LWW)** strategy with **timestamp-based resolution** will be used. Each note includes a version number and a timestamp. When syncing, the note with the later timestamp (and higher version number) will overwrite the other.
